E1: Hannibal, Hamilcaris filius, Carthaginiensis: the bare opening, like an entry in a list (name, father, nation), introduces Hannibal at once through the father whose hatred he inherits, and ends on Carthaginiensis to mark him as Rome’s great enemy
si verum est, quod nemo dubitat: the parenthesis assures Roman readers of their own supremacy before the bold claim that follows, so the praise of Hannibal carries more weight
non est infitiandum: litotes makes the praise sound undeniable, as if the facts force Nepos to admit Hannibal’s greatness

tanto praestitisse ceteros imperatores prudentia, quanto populus Romanus antecedat fortitudine cunctas nationes: the balanced tanto … quanto comparison ranks Hannibal above all generals as high as Rome stands above all nations, a powerful claim for an opening
quotienscumque cum eo congressus est in Italia, semper discessit superior: the sweeping quotienscumque … semper allows no exception, and the sentence ends emphatically on superior

quod nisi domi civium suorum invidia debilitatus esset, Romanos videtur superare potuisse: the unreal condition imagines Hannibal defeating Rome, softened by the cautious videtur, which makes his failure tragic
multorum obtrectatio devicit unius virtutem: the antithesis of many against one, and spite against courage, sums up his fate in one short, pointed sentence
velut hereditate relictum odium paternum: the metaphor of an inheritance makes hatred of Rome part of Hannibal’s identity from the start
ut prius animam quam id deposuerit: hyperbole: he would give up his life sooner than his hatred, which shows its power over him
numquam destiterit animo bellare cum Romanis: the emphatic numquam ends the introduction on his unbroken war with Rome, preparing for the rest of the Life
E1b: si verum est, quod nemo dubitat: the conditional opening and the parenthesis concede Rome’s superiority first, so Roman readers are reassured before Hannibal is praised
ut populus Romanus omnes gentes virtute superarit: Rome is said to surpass all peoples in courage, flattering the readers and setting the standard for the comparison
non est infitiandum: litotes presents the praise as reluctant but forced by the facts, so Nepos seems fair rather than disloyal

tanto praestitisse ceteros imperatores prudentia, quanto populus Romanus antecedat fortitudine cunctas nationes: the careful balance gives Hannibal prudentia and Rome fortitudo, so each side has its own virtue and Hannibal is never braver than the Romans
semper discessit superior: the strong claim of unbroken victory is confined to battles in Italy, a precise limit that keeps the praise defensible
Romanos videtur superare potuisse: the cautious videtur and the unreal condition soften the idea of a Roman defeat
domi civium suorum invidia debilitatus: Hannibal is beaten by the jealousy of his own people, so Rome’s honour is not damaged by his downfall
multorum obtrectatio devicit unius virtutem: the antithesis praises his virtus while placing the blame at Carthage
numquam destiterit animo bellare cum Romanis: the closing emphasis on his lifelong hostility reminds Roman readers that this great man was their enemy
E1c: multorum obtrectatio devicit unius virtutem: the antithesis shows Hannibal undone by others’ spite, so his own hatred of Rome stands out as the constant in his life
velut hereditate relictum odium paternum erga Romanos: the inheritance metaphor makes the hatred something he was born into, the force behind everything he does
sic conservavit, ut prius animam quam id deposuerit: the result clause and the hyperbole of giving up his life before his hatred show it outlasting everything else
cum patria pulsus esset et alienarum opum indigeret: the pair of hardships, exile and dependence, stresses that nothing could weaken his hostility
numquam destiterit animo bellare cum Romanis: the emphatic negative and animo show him at war with Rome in his mind even when he had no army
ut omittam Philippum, quem absens hostem reddidit Romanis: praeteritio still names Philip, and absens shows his hatred working even at a distance
omnium iis temporibus potentissimus rex Antiochus: the superlative and the delayed name make the king he turns against Rome as great as possible
hunc tanta cupiditate incendit bellandi: the fire metaphor in incendit presents Hannibal as the spark that sets kings alight with war
usque a rubro mari arma conatus sit inferre Italiae: the geographical extremes, ending on Italiae, show his hatred driving a war across the world towards Rome
E2: ut omittam Philippum, quem absens hostem reddidit Romanis: praeteritio lets Nepos add one more example, and absens shows that Hannibal is dangerous even from a distance
omnium iis temporibus potentissimus rex Antiochus fuit: the superlative, framed by omnium and the delayed name, magnifies the king whom Hannibal can sway
hunc tanta cupiditate incendit bellandi: the fire metaphor and the delayed bellandi present Hannibal as the spark of a new war
usque a rubro mari arma conatus sit inferre Italiae: the sweep from the Red Sea to Italy, with Italiae in final position, shows the reach of his threat to Rome
consiliis clandestinis ut Hannibalem in suspicionem regi adducerent: the alliteration of c and the secret plotting show how much the Romans fear him

neque id frustra fecissent idque Hannibal comperisset seque ab interioribus consiliis segregari vidisset: polysyndeton builds up the stages of the plot and his discovery of it, so his response comes as a climax
tempore dato adiit ad regem: the main verb arrives at last after the long periodic sentence, showing his decisive action
de fide sua et odio in Romanos: loyalty and hatred of Rome are paired, so his hatred is the proof of his loyalty
pater meus … Hamilcar puerulo me, utpote non amplius VIIII annos nato: the switch to direct speech, the diminutive puerulo and the exact age show his determination rooted in childhood
Iovi optimo maximo hostias immolavit: the solemn religious formula makes his hostility to Rome sacred and binding
E2b: qui de eius voluntate explorarent: the envoys come to spy out the king’s intentions, a furtive role for Roman ambassadors
darentque operam consiliis clandestinis: the alliteration of c binds plans and secrecy together, so the Romans appear sly and underhand
ut Hannibalem in suspicionem regi adducerent: their aim is to ruin Hannibal by suspicion, working indirectly
tamquam ab ipsis corruptus alia atque antea sentiret: irony: the Romans spread the charge that he has been bribed by them, when they are the ones acting corruptly
seque ab interioribus consiliis segregari vidisset: the vivid word choice of segregari, separated from the flock, shows the effect of the Roman plotting on Hannibal
tempore dato adiit ad regem: in contrast with the Romans’ secret plots, Hannibal goes straight to the king
multa de fide sua et odio in Romanos commemorasset: Hannibal speaks openly of his loyalty, a contrast with Roman deceit
pater meus … inquit: direct speech gives Hannibal his own voice and authority, which the Romans, seen only through their schemes, do not have
Iovi optimo maximo hostias immolavit: the solemn sacrifice sets Hannibal’s sacred, open oath against the Romans’ hidden methods
E2c: pater meus … inquit: the change to direct speech makes the scene vivid, told in Hannibal’s own words, with pater meus placed first to frame the oath as a family duty
puerulo me, utpote non amplius VIIII annos nato: the diminutive and the precise age make the boy vivid and stress how young he was
Iovi optimo maximo hostias immolavit: the formal cult title and the sacrifice of victims give the scene a solemn, religious setting
quae divina res dum conficiebatur: calling the rite a divine matter reminds the reader that the oath is sworn before the gods
id cum libenter accepissem atque ab eo petere coepissem ne dubitaret ducere: the boy’s eagerness, pleading to go, adds a lively, human touch
faciam, inquit, si mihi fidem, quam postulo, dederis: Hamilcar’s short conditional reply, in direct speech, has the force of a solemn contract
simul me ad aram adduxit: simul quickens the pace, so the action follows at once
eamque ceteris remotis tenentem: the private setting and the physical detail of the boy holding the altar make the scene easy to picture and sacred
iurare iussit numquam me in amicitia cum Romanis fore: the emphatic numquam makes the oath absolute and lifelong
E3: quae divina res dum conficiebatur: the religious setting gives the story authority, since the oath was sworn in the presence of the gods
id cum libenter accepissem atque ab eo petere coepissem ne dubitaret ducere: the boy’s eagerness persuades the king that hatred of Rome was Hannibal’s own choice from the start
faciam, inquit, si mihi fidem, quam postulo, dederis: direct speech and the key word fidem remind Antiochus that Hannibal’s good faith was pledged before the gods
eamque ceteris remotis tenentem iurare iussit: vivid physical detail makes the account believable and the oath binding
numquam me in amicitia cum Romanis fore: the emphatic negative makes the oath absolute, answering the suspicion that he has changed sides
id ego iusiurandum patri datum usque ad hanc aetatem ita conservavi: the emphatic id ego and usque ad hanc aetatem turn his whole life into proof of his loyalty
ut nemini dubium esse debeat, quin reliquo tempore eadem mente sim futurus: the result clause argues from past to future, so his record guarantees his loyalty
si quid amice de Romanis cogitabis, non imprudenter feceris, si me celaris: litotes makes his advice tactful when speaking to a king
te ipsum frustraberis, si non me in eo principem posueris: the blunt warning and the final emphasis on principem end his case with a confident claim to command
E3b: quaesivit a me, vellemne secum in castra proficisci: Hamilcar asks rather than orders, so the father offers the son a choice
id cum libenter accepissem atque ab eo petere coepissem ne dubitaret ducere: the roles reverse: the son ends up pleading with the father, showing his eagerness to follow him
faciam, inquit, si mihi fidem, quam postulo, dederis: Hamilcar’s short, conditional reply in direct speech shows his authority and makes the bond a solemn bargain
simul me ad aram adduxit: simul shows the father acting at once and leading the boy
apud quam sacrificare instituerat: the boy is brought into his father’s own sacrifice, joining him in a sacred act
eamque ceteris remotis tenentem iurare iussit: the ablative absolute makes the oath private, a bond between father and son alone, and iussit stresses the father’s command
numquam me in amicitia cum Romanis fore: the absolute negative shows the father passing on his lifelong hatred
id ego iusiurandum patri datum: patri datum shows the oath as something owed to his father, kept out of loyalty to him
usque ad hanc aetatem ita conservavi: the length of time stresses how deeply the father’s influence has shaped the son’s whole life
E3c: id ego iusiurandum patri datum usque ad hanc aetatem ita conservavi: the emphatic ego and his lifelong constancy present him as a man of firm resolve
ut nemini dubium esse debeat, quin reliquo tempore eadem mente sim futurus: the confident result clause shows him sure of himself
non imprudenter feceris, si me celaris: litotes shows the tact of a leader handling a king
te ipsum frustraberis, si non me in eo principem posueris: he tells a king bluntly that he would be fooling himself, and ends his speech on principem, a claim to command
hac igitur, qua diximus, aetate cum patre in Hispaniam profectus est: Nepos rounds off the story and returns to the start of his career at the age of nine
cuius post obitum, Hasdrubale imperatore suffecto, equitatui omni praefuit: the compressed ablative absolutes move quickly to his first command, of all the cavalry
hoc quoque interfecto exercitus summam imperii ad eum detulit: the army itself chooses him for supreme command, a sign of a natural leader
id Carthaginem delatum publice comprobatum est: the repetition of detulit … delatum links the soldiers’ choice to its official approval, showing that his leadership was recognised by all
E4: sic Hannibal minor quinque et viginti annis natus imperator factus: the precise detail of his age stresses how young he was to command
proximo triennio omnes gentes Hispaniae bello subegit: the hyperbole of omnes and the short time span stress the speed and scale of his conquests
Saguntum, foederatam civitatem, vi expugnavit, tres exercitus maximos comparavit: asyndeton piles up his achievements, and the superlative maximos adds to their scale

ex his unum in Africam misit, alterum cum Hasdrubale fratre in Hispania reliquit, tertium in Italiam secum duxit: the tricolon unum … alterum … tertium shows a commander planning on three fronts at once, climaxing in Italy
quacumque iter fecit, cum omnibus incolis conflixit: neminem nisi victum dimisit: the sweeping quacumque and omnibus and the emphatic negative neminem allow no exception to his victories
quas nemo umquam cum exercitu ante eum praeter Herculem Graium transierat: the double negative nemo umquam and the comparison with Hercules raise his feat to heroic level
Alpicos conantes prohibere transitu concidit: the strong verb concidit shows how he cut down all opposition
loca patefecit, itinera muniit, effecit: the asyndeton of short verbs conveys his energy and his skill as an engineer

ut ea elephantus ornatus ire posset, qua antea unus homo inermis vix poterat repere: the contrast of a fully equipped elephant with a single unarmed man who could barely crawl shows the scale of what he achieved
E4b: tertium in Italiam secum duxit: the climax of the tricolon of armies places Italy and Hannibal’s own march at the centre of the story
saltum Pyrenaeum transiit: the bare statement of crossing the Pyrenees makes a great feat sound routine, preparing for the greater one
neminem nisi victum dimisit: the emphatic negative shows him conquering all who stood in his way
quae Italiam ab Gallia seiungunt: the Alps are presented as a barrier dividing nations, raising the stakes of the crossing
quas nemo umquam cum exercitu ante eum praeter Herculem Graium transierat: the double negative and the comparison with Hercules make the crossing heroic and nearly unique
quo facto is hodie saltus Graius appellatur: the reference to the pass still bearing the hero’s name gives the achievement a legendary quality
Alpicos conantes prohibere transitu concidit: the vivid verb concidit shows him cutting down the tribes who resisted
loca patefecit, itinera muniit, effecit: asyndeton of three short verbs conveys relentless effort

elephantus ornatus ire posset, qua antea unus homo inermis vix poterat repere: the contrast of a laden elephant with one unarmed man barely crawling, stressed by vix and repere, shows how hard the route had been
hac copias traduxit in Italiamque pervenit: the short closing sentence marks the achievement of the goal
E4c: cuius post obitum, Hasdrubale imperatore suffecto, equitatui omni praefuit: the compressed ablative absolutes pass quickly over events, so his first command arrives almost at once
hoc quoque interfecto exercitus summam imperii ad eum detulit: another brief ablative absolute moves straight to his supreme command
id Carthaginem delatum publice comprobatum est: the short sentence shows Carthage confirming his appointment without delay
minor quinque et viginti annis natus imperator factus: the precise age stresses how young he was when he took command
proximo triennio omnes gentes Hispaniae bello subegit: the short time span and omnes convey the speed and sweep of his conquest of Spain
Saguntum, foederatam civitatem, vi expugnavit, tres exercitus maximos comparavit: asyndeton lists achievements rapidly, one after another
ex his unum in Africam misit, alterum cum Hasdrubale fratre in Hispania reliquit, tertium in Italiam secum duxit: the brisk tricolon shows armies dispatched in quick succession
saltum Pyrenaeum transiit, quacumque iter fecit, cum omnibus incolis conflixit: short clauses in asyndeton keep the march moving at speed
neminem nisi victum dimisit: the emphatic negative closes the passage on unbroken success
E5: conflixerat apud Rhodanum cum P. Cornelio Scipione consule eumque pepulerat: the first victory over a consul is told in a single brisk sentence, setting the pattern of the chapter
cum hoc eodem Clastidi apud Padum decernit sauciumque inde ac fugatum dimittit: the historic present makes the second victory vivid, and the paired participles show the same consul wounded and routed
tertio idem Scipio cum collega Tiberio Longo apud Trebiam adversus eum venit: tertio and idem stress that the same enemy kept coming back to be beaten
cum his manum conseruit, utrosque profligavit: asyndeton and the strong verb profligavit make the victory over both commanders sound instant and total
qua valetudine cum etiam tum premeretur lecticaque ferretur: even ill and carried in a litter he wins, which makes his victories seem all the more overwhelming
C. Flaminium consulem apud Trasumenum cum exercitu insidiis circumventum occidit: a consul and his whole army are trapped and killed in one sentence
neque multo post C. Centenium praetorem cum delecta manu saltus occupantem: neque multo post adds another victory in quick succession
utriusque exercitus uno proelio fugavit: the contrast of two armies with a single battle shows the scale of the victory at Cannae
Paulum consulem occidit et aliquot praeterea consulares, in his Cn. Servilium Geminum, qui superiore anno fuerat consul: the list of slain consuls and ex-consuls builds to a climax of Roman losses
E5b: cum P. Cornelio Scipione consule eumque pepulerat: the consul is named in full and then simply driven back, his rank making his defeat more striking
sauciumque inde ac fugatum dimittit: the paired participles show the same consul wounded and put to flight, and dimittit suggests Hannibal letting him go at will
tertio idem Scipio cum collega Tiberio Longo apud Trebiam adversus eum venit: tertio idem makes Scipio return for a third defeat, persistent but unsuccessful
cum his manum conseruit, utrosque profligavit: the two commanders are crushed together in two short clauses
C. Flaminium consulem apud Trasumenum cum exercitu insidiis circumventum occidit: the consul falls into an ambush with his army, outwitted and killed
C. Centenium praetorem cum delecta manu saltus occupantem: even a praetor with a picked force holding the pass is overcome
ibi obviam ei venerunt duo consules, C. Terentius et L. Aemilius: the two consuls are named as they march out to meet him, building expectation
utriusque exercitus uno proelio fugavit: the contrast between two consular armies and one battle shows the commanders’ helplessness
Paulum consulem occidit et aliquot praeterea consulares: the list of fallen consuls and ex-consuls presents the Roman leadership as repeatedly beaten, however senior its men
E5c: inde per Ligures Appenninum transiit, petens Etruriam: another mountain range is crossed in a single clause, as if nothing could stop him
hoc itinere adeo gravi morbo afficitur oculorum: the historic present and adeo gravi make his illness vivid and show his human weakness
ut postea numquam dextro aeque bene usus sit: the result clause and numquam stress a lasting injury, the cost of the campaign to him
qua valetudine cum etiam tum premeretur lecticaque ferretur: the image of the general carried in a litter shows how ill he was, making what follows more remarkable
C. Flaminium consulem apud Trasumenum cum exercitu insidiis circumventum occidit: straight after the litter comes the ambush and death of a consul and his army, so the sick man is still unstoppable
neque multo post C. Centenium praetorem cum delecta manu saltus occupantem: neque multo post adds another quick victory
hinc in Apuliam pervenit: the short sentence keeps the advance moving
utriusque exercitus uno proelio fugavit: the contrast of two armies and one battle shows his overwhelming power
Paulum consulem occidit et aliquot praeterea consulares: the climax of Roman losses ends the passage on his unstoppable success
E6: hic clausus locorum angustiis noctu sine ullo detrimento exercitus se expedivit: the trap and the escape without any loss are set side by side, so his cunning gets him out of an impossible position
Fabioque, callidissimo imperatori, dedit verba: the superlative praises Fabius as the cleverest of commanders in the very clause where Hannibal fools him, so Hannibal seems cleverer still
obducta nocte sarmenta in cornibus iuvencorum deligata incendit: the vivid detail of burning brushwood tied to the cattle’s horns shows an ingenious trick
eiusque generis multitudinem magnam dispalatam immisit: the great scattered herd shows the scale of the deception
quo repentino visu obiecto tantum terrorem iniecit exercitui Romanorum: repentino and tantum terrorem stress the sudden fear his trick causes
ut egredi extra vallum nemo sit ausus: the result clause ends on nemo sit ausus: a whole Roman army is pinned down by a trick
M. Minucium Rufum, magistrum equitum pari ac dictatorem imperio, dolo productum in proelium fugavit: dolo productum shows him luring a senior commander into battle by deceit
Ti. Sempronium Gracchum, iterum consulem, in Lucanis absens in insidias inductum sustulit: absens shows his cunning working even at a distance
M. Claudium Marcellum, quinquies consulem, apud Venusiam pari modo interfecit: pari modo makes ambush his signature method
nemo ei in acie restitit, nemo adversus eum post Cannensem pugnam in campo castra posuit: the anaphora of nemo shows that the Romans no longer dared to face him
E6b: hac pugna pugnata Romam profectus est nullo resistente: the ablative absolutes and nullo resistente show Hannibal marching on Rome unopposed, raising the tension
in propinquis urbi montibus moratus est: the image of him waiting in the hills near the city keeps the threat hanging over Rome
Q. Fabius Maximus, dictator Romanus, in agro Falerno ei se obiecit: the full name and title build up Fabius as a formidable opponent, and se obiecit shows him blocking the way
hic clausus locorum angustiis: the trap in the narrow ground creates a dramatic crisis
noctu sine ullo detrimento exercitus se expedivit: the sudden escape by night without any loss resolves the crisis at once
Fabioque, callidissimo imperatori, dedit verba: the irony of the cleverest commander being fooled adds to the drama
obducta nocte sarmenta in cornibus iuvencorum deligata incendit: the vivid picture of blazing brushwood on cattle’s horns in the dark makes the scene striking
quo repentino visu obiecto tantum terrorem iniecit exercitui Romanorum: the sudden sight and the great terror show the effect on the watching Romans
ut egredi extra vallum nemo sit ausus: the episode ends on the paralysed Roman army, the climax of Hannibal’s trick
E6c: M. Minucium Rufum, magistrum equitum pari ac dictatorem imperio, dolo productum in proelium fugavit: the rank of each defeated Roman is given in full, so every victory is over a great commander
Ti. Sempronium Gracchum, iterum consulem: iterum consulem stresses the experience of the man he destroys
in Lucanis absens in insidias inductum sustulit: absens shows him defeating a consul without even being there
M. Claudium Marcellum, quinquies consulem, apud Venusiam pari modo interfecit: the climax of the list is a five-times consul, killed in the same way
longum est omnia enumerare proelia: Nepos claims there are too many battles to list, implying that his victories are countless
quare hoc unum satis erit dictum, ex quo intellegi possit, quantus ille fuerit: hoc unum and quantus ille introduce one decisive fact as proof of his greatness
quamdiu in Italia fuit, nemo ei in acie restitit: the sweeping quamdiu and nemo cover his whole time in Italy
nemo adversus eum post Cannensem pugnam in campo castra posuit: the anaphora of nemo builds to the claim that no Roman dared even to camp against him in open country
